activity.title: As I continue my journey into tech and begin this new chapter as an EECS student at UC Berkeley, I'm truly honored to have participated in Berkeley's Pre-Engineering Program. Over three weeks, my team and I worked through the SPRINT design process — from identifying our problem, urban heat islands, to prototyping a Persian windcatcher: a passive, no-electricity cooling structure inspired by traditional Persian architecture that channels airflow downward to cool the surrounding area. Along the way, I used tools like CAD, Python, and product design to turn an idea into something that can actually help people, culminating in a final pitch to industry professionals from Anduril Industries to ex-Meta engineers. Thank you to my teammates for their hard work and collaboration: Estefania Gamboa , Johnathan Campos , Aida Jacqueline Matias Marroquin , and Sarah Ibarra . None of this would have been possible without Britt Mazorra , Marvin J. Lopez , and Oscar Dubon — thank you for supporting incoming students. And a final thank you to our design assistant Nina Nguyen , along with William Lopez Rodas and Lily Nguyen . ...more

I choose freedom. Our life is made up of actions. Each action begins with a choice. We wake up. We can snooze and stay in bed — or get up and let the sun hit our face. We feel anxious. We can doomscroll to escape reality — or sit in silence and confront it. We walk into a room of strangers. We can hide behind our phone — or simply say "hi" to the person next to us. Freedom. Freedom from dissatisfaction. Freedom from insecurity. Freedom to do anything you want. It's not found by getting rich, being liked, or "finding yourself." It's one step away: a single choice. Choose fear and sink into suffocating comfort— or choose discomfort and destroy a barrier that only ever existed in your head. It's your turn to choose. ...more ...more

Since SoCal Deep Tech Week 2024, building and supporting the deep tech community has been a labor of love. And a coalition of the willing... Working alongside operators, combat veterans, technical founders, and investors has sharpened what "Mission" actually means: delivering capability to the end operator, without fail. As an ecosystem, we know how to innovate. Where we get stuck is moving that innovation from prototype to full-rate production. So how we win is clear line of sight. The capability, the buyer, and the operator all able to see each other and address what's working and what's not. Pouring more money into a dysfunctional process doesn't fix it. Which is why we're hosting the inaugural New York National Security Forum on September 28–29, 2026 in New York City. Two days, one room, the people who build capability and the people who buy it. Request your seat at nynsf.com . We'll see you there. ...more ...more

What does it look like to actualize a dream? While acting on dreams, I feel like fear is always present no matter what. I think it always leads to the most common failure: inaction. Inaction seems to stop so many dreamers on their paths, pushing them into modern culture where we are incentivized to live a life that minimizes real risk and therefore real life. Our souls (sometimes unknowingly) become suffocated by safety, blindly following the status quo. The truth is, we will fall into this failure 10/10 times if we are not driven towards the one thing that can destroy fear. This one motivation allows us to act, and act endlessly with intention. This true freedom is the dream and success itself. So, why do we continually allow ourselves to be controlled and sometimes driven by fear, leading to dreams that will never be actualized, when there is the immediate opportunity to actualize our dream just one finger's extension away? ...more ...more

I'm not a fan of deep learning. At least the one I see most commonly. Real Deep Learning is the kind pioneered by people who deeply understand optimisation, geometry, and why gradients behave the way they do. However, the deep learning most people practice is one where they scale up a network, throw more data at it, and hope the loss goes down. That's not engineering. That's prayer with GPUs (and thanks to you why Nvidia nearly has a $5T market cap). I'm much more on the inductive bias side. Classical ML, carefully chosen priors, models that actually reflect what you know about the data. Your dataset is almost never as big as you think it is, and the structure you encode is the structure you don't have to learn from scratch. The uncomfortable truth is that model choice is often the least interesting decision in the stack. If your data is bad, no architecture saves you. If your data is good, a linear model often gets 90% of the way there and most people never bother to look. The best DL paper I've read recently is LeJEPA by Yann LeCun and collaborators. Real maths. Real priors. Not a single mention of "just add more layers." That's the deep learning I have time for the kind where the architecture means something. Garbage in, garbage out. Generative garbage in, generative garbage out. Agentic garbage in... well, you get the idea. ...more ...more

This summer, I had the honor of being one of the first Chemical Engineers to participate in the PREP Pre-Engineering Program at UC Berkeley alongside George Santiago Luna and Estefani Esther Esqueda Galvez . PREP is a three-week summer intensive program that guides incoming engineers by focusing on three main topics: the academic rigor at UC Berkeley, product development through CAD and 3D printing to solve a real-world problem, and the fundamentals of networking and professionalism. I would like to thank my team members, Sergio Carrillo Martinez , Marvin Gregory Singleton , Isabella Rosas , and Esmeralda Martinez, for their dedication, hard work, and inclusiveness throughout the program. I hope to be able to continue being someone they can count on throughout the next four years at UC Berkeley. I would also like to thank Britt Mazorra and Marvin J. Lopez for including College of Chemistry engineering students and planning such a wonderful program that gives us first-year students "a leg up" as we approach our first year at Berkeley. I am grateful for the many speakers who were able to give us insight into different aspects of engineering and student life at Berkeley, including David Yee , whose story of resilience and perseverance inspires me to push forward during times of hardship. And finally, a special thank you to my calculus teacher, Galilea Gonzalez , for teaching me how to approach the rigors of UC Berkeley math and sharing her insights into different study habits and strategies that led to her success. I would also like to thank my dormitory floor's Resident Assistant, William Lopez Rodas , who created a welcoming environment and shared his background and accomplishments, inspiring me to strive for similar success during my next four years at Cal. The memories made during this program are unforgettable, and I am looking forward to seeing the 2026 PREP Cohort again in the fall! Go Bears! 🐻

Late 2025, a few trusted friends and I started to discuss the bottlenecks that exist preventing emerging technologies from being adopted across the joint force. The conversations kept landing in the same place: the technology exists. The demand exists. The capital exists. What's missing is a focused room where the people behind all three actually work the problem together. So Peter Downes , Jay V. , Saptarsi B. , Diana Skurka and I are bringing that room together. The inaugural New York National Security Forum is set for September 28–29. Two days, invitation only, every session under Chatham House Rules. Day One works the demand side: how the institutions that buy capability actually decide. Day Two works the capital side: how the money that funds this market thinks. I keep seeing the same thing in Kyiv and beyond: ecosystems and partnerships are part of the logic that turns discrete technologies into fielded capabilities and battlefield effects. The Forum exists to build that ecosystem here. Attendance is by application: NYNSF.com Venue and first speakers announced soon. See you in September. #NationalSecurity #DefenseTech #EmergingTech #NewYork

first generation filipina from sfv going to berkeley engineering 😍👏👏🤪🤪 wait… FIRST gen FILIPINA from SFV…. going to BERKELEY ENGINEERING 😟😰😰 This past March, I opened my laptop to discover my acceptance to UC Berkeley. Initially, I had trouble accepting this merit, and my jubilation was (slightly) inhibited by intimidation: how am I going to survive at the #1 public university & #3 engineering program in the world? ?!!?!!!! However, I later received more great news that I was accepted into the Pre-Engineering Program (PREP), for which I’ve had the privilege and pleasure to participate in a 3-week intensive, developing my academic and professional skills to acclimate to the UC Berkeley rigor. The summit of my experience occurred on July 31st: the Maker Design Expo. In just ~26 hours of instructional time, I gained hands-on experience in Arduino, CAD, C++, and 3D printing to develop Nexus: a wearable fall-detection device designed to aid users while reducing medical costs. That day, my team — Ubah Ismail , Pedro Terrero Chavez , Jefferson Martinez , Barbara Avalos , and I — proudly engineered and presented our prototype. I’d like to express my appreciation for Scott Moura and Sebastian Castañeda Guerrero for leading us through the Maker Design Studio. Your wisdom and dedication are a huge inspiration. A special ‘thank you’ to our Design Assistant, Alan Romero . Your advocacy and encouragement fostered our success! I am honored to be part of a program of such outstanding individuals, as each student in my cohort feels like family. A special thanks to the Learning Fascilitator, Galilea Gonzalez : your compassionate guidance has given me the self-assurance to thrive academically. Additionally, a huge ‘thank you’ to the Residential Assistants, Estela Jauregui Jauregui and William Lopez Rodas , for your kind mentorship and support as leaders in PREP. You all made this summer incredibly memorable. Ultimately, I am sincerely grateful to Marvin J. Lopez & Britt Mazorra for organizing this program. This opportunity has allowed me to find my community, my belonging, and my home at Berkeley. 🐻💛 (& shout out to jude BELLINGHAM) #FirstGeneration #WomenInSTEM #UCBerkeley #SanFernandoValley

My journey with UC Berkeley Pre-Engineering Program (PREP) came full circle this summer. After participating as a student in the PREP class of 2025, I was honored to return to the program as a Residential Assistant for the incoming class of 2026. This transition allowed me to contribute to a community that has been foundational to my own engineering career. PREP is an intensive three-week program designed to support first-generation college students by providing them with a robust professional network and introducing them to the vast resources within UC Berkeley Engineering. A cornerstone of the experience is the SPRINT project design competition. During this competition, students develop essential technical skills—including programming, CAD, and prototyping—to create functional solutions for real-world problems, which they eventually present to a panel of judges. Serving as a Residential Assistant, I worked alongside William Lopez Rodas , Yulia Yang , Joaquin Cabrera Caballero , and Floormate Milagros Perez Mejia to support our students within the residential halls. Over the course of the program, I witnessed a remarkable transformation as the students acclimated to the Berkeley lifestyle and grew into confident, driven individuals. It was a privilege to mentor the PREP cohort of 2026 and observe their professional and personal development firsthand. I would like to extend my sincere gratitude to my supervisors, Britt Mazorra and Marvin J. Lopez , for their leadership in hosting such a successful program. I am also grateful to everyone who supports PREP, ensuring it continues to provide vital opportunities for aspiring engineers. Finally, congratulations to the PREP class of 2026 on taking this significant first step into Berkeley Engineering. Go Bears!

Add "accidentally playing against my teachers" to the list of things I didn't expect to do before graduating. It wasn't on my senior bucket list. I wasn't even planning on playing. And yet somehow, there I was, running up and down the court against the same teachers I'd spent four years learning from. Looking back, it's kind of funny how many of my favorite senior year memories happened because of things I never planned for. The schedule, the grades, the milestones, the many senior events… those were easy to predict. But the random moments that became the funny stories I'd actually tell afterward? Not so much.
